# Ordinal Equivalence Under EVSDT

## Coordinate systems

Let $H$ and $F$ denote the hit (true positive) and false alarm (false positive) rates. Define Positive Predictive Bias (PPB) $= H + F$ and Youden’s $J = H - F$. Then the map $(H, F) \mapsto (J, \text{PPB}) = (H - F,\; H + F)$ is a bijection on the unit square with inverse $H = (J + \text{PPB})/2$, $F = (\text{PPB} - J)/2$.

Under equal-variance Gaussian signal detection theory (EVSDT), the standard parameters $(d', c)$ arise from the same rotation applied after a coordinate-wise probit transform:

$$d' = z(H) - z(F), \qquad -2c = z(H) + z(F)$$ {#eq-sdt-supp}

where $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard-normal cumulative distribution and density functions, respectively, and $z = \Phi^{-1}$ is the quantile (probit) function. Both pairs use a difference and a sum with perpendicular rows. The $(J, \text{PPB})$ map is orthogonal up to the factor $\sqrt{2}$; $(d', c)$ scales the two rows unequally. The pairs operate in observed-rate and probit-transformed space, respectively.

## Monotonicity proofs

Under EVSDT the noise distribution is $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and the signal distribution $\mathcal{N}(d', 1)$. Write $\theta$ for the criterion's location on that latent axis, so $H = \Phi(d' - \theta)$ and $F = \Phi(-\theta)$. @eq-sdt-supp then gives $c = \theta - d'/2$: $c$ locates the criterion relative to the midpoint between the two means, which is the convention of the main text and of @macmillan_response_1990. Substituting $\theta = c + d'/2$,

$$J(d', c) = \Phi(d'/2 - c) - \Phi(-d'/2 - c), \qquad \text{PPB}(d', c) = \Phi(d'/2 - c) + \Phi(-d'/2 - c)$$

$J$ is strictly increasing in $d'$ at fixed $c$:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial d'} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[\phi(d'/2 - c) + \phi(-d'/2 - c)\right] > 0$$ {#eq-j-mono}

since $\phi(\cdot) > 0$ everywhere (@eq-j-mono). Thus, at fixed $c$, ordering observers by $J$ coincides with ordering by $d'$.

PPB is strictly decreasing in $c$ at fixed $d'$:

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial c} = -\phi(d'/2 - c) - \phi(-d'/2 - c) < 0$$ {#eq-ppb-mono}

since both terms are strictly negative (@eq-ppb-mono). Thus, at fixed $d'$, ordering observers by PPB coincides with ordering by $-c$, the reverse ordering of $c$.

Across observers who differ on both dimensions simultaneously, the two coordinate systems can rank observers differently (see main text).

## Criterion interpretation beyond EVSDT

The computed index $c = -\frac{1}{2}[z(H) + z(F)]$ is defined when both rates lie in $(0,1)$.

Under EVSDT the computed $c$ recovers the criterion exactly: $c = -\frac{1}{2}[\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(d' - \theta)) + \Phi^{-1}(\Phi(-\theta))] = \theta - d'/2$, a fixed offset from $\theta$.

For general evidence distributions, let $G_n$ and $G_s$ denote the cumulative distribution functions of noise and signal evidence. An observer with criterion $\theta$ produces $H = 1 - G_s(\theta)$ and $F = 1 - G_n(\theta)$. The computed $c$ becomes

$$c_{\text{comp}} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\Phi^{-1}(1 - G_s(\theta)) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - G_n(\theta))\bigr]$$

At interior rates, its relation to $\theta$ depends on the shapes of $G_s$ and $G_n$. Two observers with the same criterion $\theta$ but different latent distributions (e.g., Gaussian vs.\ logistic, or equal vs.\ unequal variance) will generally produce different values of $c_{\text{comp}}$, because the probit transforms rates generated by different evidence distributions onto the same standard-normal scale.

At interior rates, both coordinate pairs remain invertible transformations of $(H, F)$. PPB alone does not determine computed $c$ without $J$. Outside EVSDT, $c_{\text{comp}}$ need not recover centered criterion location in Gaussian units. It remains monotone in criterion when the evidence distributions are held fixed, but its values need not identify a common centered location across distributions. PPB remains twice the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation, without assumptions about latent evidence distributions.

**Worked example.** Consider four distribution families, each with signal location $\mu = 2$ and noise location 0, with criteria $\theta$ chosen so that PPB $= H + F = 1.20$ exactly. The $t(3)$ distribution is scaled to unit variance. The common location shift does not hold discriminability constant across distributions with different variances and tails. Matching PPB fixes the sum of the two rates but leaves their difference, $J$, free to vary.

| Distribution | Parameters | $\theta$ | $H$ | $F$ | PPB | $J$ | $c_{\text{comp}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian EV | $\sigma_s = \sigma_n = 1$ | 0.587 | 0.921 | 0.279 | 1.20 | 0.642 | $-0.413$ |
| Logistic | $s = 1$ | 0.487 | 0.819 | 0.381 | 1.20 | 0.439 | $-0.305$ |
| Gaussian UV | $\sigma_s = 2, \sigma_n = 1$ | 0.270 | 0.806 | 0.394 | 1.20 | 0.413 | $-0.297$ |
| $t(3)$ (scaled) | $\text{Var} = 1$ | 0.468 | 0.962 | 0.238 | 1.20 | 0.723 | $-0.529$ |

All four observers have the same PPB (1.20), but $J$ ranges from $0.413$ to $0.723$ and computed $c$ from $-0.53$ to $-0.30$, moving monotonically with $J$. Matching the families on both $H$ and $F$, which each of them permits (two free parameters, location and criterion, against two constraints), makes $J$, PPB, $c$ and every other function of $(H, F)$ agree exactly.

## PPB as the criterion of the equal-variance uniform model

Let the noise distribution be uniform on $[0, 1]$ and the signal distribution uniform on $[\delta, 1 + \delta]$, with $0 \le \delta \le 1$; this is double high-threshold theory written as a pair of latent distributions [@macmillan_response_1990]. An observer says yes when the evidence exceeds the criterion $\theta$ on the latent axis (§1.2). Macmillan and Creelman’s $k$ denotes the centered index $c_{\text{rect}}$. For $\delta < \theta < 1$ both rates are interior to $(0, 1)$, and

$$F = 1 - \theta, \qquad H = 1 - (\theta - \delta) = 1 - \theta + \delta$$ {#eq-rect-rates}

Differencing @eq-rect-rates gives $J = H - F = \delta$: Youden's $J$ recovers the separation between the two distributions. This is Macmillan and Creelman's Equation 16 (1990, p. 406), $q = H - F = 2p(c) - 1$, and it is also Snodgrass and Corwin's [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] double high-threshold discrimination index $P_r$. Summing @eq-rect-rates instead,

$$\text{PPB} = H + F = 2 - 2\theta + \delta, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \theta = \frac{2 + \delta - \text{PPB}}{2}$$ {#eq-rect-sum}

The two distribution means are $1/2$ and $1/2 + \delta$, so the midpoint between them is $(1 + \delta)/2$, and the criterion measured from that midpoint is

$$c_{\text{rect}} = \theta - \frac{1 + \delta}{2} = \frac{2 + \delta - \text{PPB}}{2} - \frac{1 + \delta}{2} = \frac{1 - \text{PPB}}{2}$$ {#eq-crect-supp}

@eq-crect-supp is Macmillan and Creelman's Equation 17 (1990, p. 406), $k = 0.5[1 - (F + H)]$, exactly: their $k$ is this centered index, not the raw criterion $\theta$. The discriminability parameter has dropped out of the centered criterion expression: at a fixed $c_{\text{rect}}$, PPB is constant as $\delta$ varies within the overlap region. This is parameter separation under the model, not statistical independence or a prediction about which criterion observers hold fixed.

@eq-crect-supp holds for $\delta \le \theta \le 1$, including the endpoints. Outside that interval, a rate equals 0 or 1, so $J$ need not recover $\delta$ and $(1-\text{PPB})/2$ need not locate the actual centered criterion, although the transform remains defined. Boundary rates do not always prevent criterion identification: under the restriction $0 \le \delta \le 1$, $H=1$ and $F=0$ force $\delta=\theta=1$. If the model is extended to $\delta>1$, any criterion in $[1,\delta]$ produces those perfect rates.

PPB/2 equals the overall proportion of "yes" responses, $\pi H + (1 - \pi)F$ for signal probability $\pi$, when $\pi = 1/2$ (or when $H=F$). This equality under equal presentation is the basis of Macmillan and Creelman’s yes rate. The criterion reading itself does not require $\pi = 1/2$, because the formula uses conditional rates. Changing prevalence may nevertheless change those rates through the observer's decision rule.

@decarlo_signal_1998 shows that signal detection models are generalized linear models: the observed rates are passed through a link function, and $d'$ is a difference and the criterion, up to scale, is a sum of the link-transformed rates,

$$d' = z(H) - z(F), \qquad c = -\tfrac{1}{2}[z(H) + z(F)]$$ {#eq-links}

with $z = \Phi^{-1}$ the probit link. Substituting the affine link $z(p) = p - \tfrac{1}{2}$, which is the identity link with the origin moved to balanced response propensity, gives

$$\left(H - \tfrac{1}{2}\right) - \left(F - \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = J, \qquad -\tfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(H - \tfrac{1}{2}\right) + \left(F - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{1 - \text{PPB}}{2} = c_{\text{rect}}$$ {#eq-identity-link}

@eq-identity-link and @eq-links compute the same pair of contrasts under two links. The shift by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ cancels in the difference and adds a constant to the sum. With the identity link proper, $z(p) = p$, the contrasts give $J$ and $-\text{PPB}/2$; the uncentered bias contrast equals $-1/2$ when PPB $= 1$. The linear link preserves computability at boundary rates, exact aggregation, and additive covariate effects in probability units (§§2--4). Macmillan and Creelman also report a binomial sampling result for the yes rate, attributed to Morgan. Sampling distributions depend on trial allocation: §5 distinguishes random trial-type allocation from the fixed signal and noise counts used here.

## The Snodgrass and Corwin invariance test applied to PPB

Snodgrass and Corwin's [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] Table 3 reports cell means for the six conditions of their $2 \times 3$ design (word imagery $\times$ payoff matrix). PPB is the sum of the hit and false alarm rows, and $c_{\text{rect}} = (1 - \text{PPB})/2$ expresses it in uniform-model criterion units. The $C$ they report is Gaussian $c$, as in the main text; Gaussian and uniform criterion measures use different units.

| Payoff | $H$ (high, low) | $F$ (high, low) | PPB (high, low) | $c_{\text{rect}}$ gap | $c$ gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conservative | 0.716, 0.474 | 0.097, 0.203 | 0.813, 0.677 | $-0.068$ | $-0.122$ |
| Neutral | 0.826, 0.632 | 0.161, 0.303 | 0.987, 0.935 | $-0.026$ | $-0.053$ |
| Liberal | 0.868, 0.723 | 0.219, 0.397 | 1.087, 1.120 | $+0.017$ | $+0.001$ |

: Snodgrass and Corwin (1988), Table 3: PPB $= H+F$ from cell mean rates, and high-minus-low imagery gaps in $c_{\text{rect}}=(1-\text{PPB})/2$ and reported Gaussian $c$. Gaps use each index’s criterion units. {#tbl-sc-invariance}

Their test asks whether a bias index shows a payoff effect, no imagery effect and no interaction. The payoff effect is large for PPB, which moves from about 0.75 to about 1.10 as the payoff goes from conservative to liberal. The imagery gaps in @tbl-sc-invariance are the quantity their test requires to be null. Their directions differ across payoff conditions. Their numerical magnitudes cannot compare invariance across the two criterion scales. For $c$, the original subject-level analysis found no significant imagery or interaction effect.

These condition means lack the participant-level variances and covariances needed for the within-subjects tests, so they cannot determine whether PPB would meet Snodgrass and Corwin’s ANOVA criteria. Mean PPB equals PPB computed from mean rates. For $B_r$ and $c$, those summaries generally differ.

### The test on open subject-level data

*Layher, Dixit and Miller* [-@layher_who_2020], OSF project 4k2hb, files `layher20_exp1.csv` and `layher20_exp2.csv` (session-level counts; the trial-level file for Experiment 1 reproduces every count). In each experiment 39 participants took old/new face-recognition tests in ten sessions, having studied the faces once in five sessions and five times in the other five. In Experiment 1 the bias manipulation was a payoff matrix (conservative, neutral, liberal), with 500 targets and 500 lures per participant and cell. The five-presentation sessions were always sessions 6--10, so strength is confounded with practice. In Experiment 2 the bias manipulation was the proportion of old items at test (25, 50 or 75\%), with 1,000 trials per participant and cell, and the order of the strength conditions was counterbalanced (20 and 19 participants).

*Measuring Memory Project* [@starns_assessing_2019], OSF project 92ahy, file `Data/data_full.csv`, conditions decoded from `dataKey_full.pdf`. Each of 459 participants studied a word list once, twice or three times and received no bias instruction, a conservative instruction or a liberal instruction (nine between-subjects cells of 48--53), then made old/new decisions on 50 targets and 50 lures. I used the binary responses.

For each participant and cell, PPB and $J$ use raw rates. I computed $c$, $d'$ and $B_r$ with the log-linear correction $(x + 0.5)/(N + 1)$, which Snodgrass and Corwin recommend for every index. Raw $B_r$ is $0/0$ for two Measuring Memory participants. Layher et al.'s designs were analysed by two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance, with each effect tested against its own subject-by-effect error term and no sphericity correction; the Measuring Memory design by two-way between-subjects analysis of variance with Type III sums of squares. The ANOVA-criteria column applies Snodgrass and Corwin’s criteria at $\alpha = .05$: a bias index passes if the bias effect is significant and neither the strength effect nor the interaction is; $J$ and $d'$, discrimination indexes, pass if the strength effect is significant and neither the bias effect nor the interaction is. A pass means that the index met these criteria; it does not establish equivalence or invariance.

PPB and $J$ use raw rates; $c$, $d'$ and $B_r$ use log-linear rates unless otherwise marked. ^a^ Two participants with $H=1$, $F=0$, for whom raw $B_r$ is undefined, are excluded ($N = 457$; error df 448). {#tbl-inv-mm}

PPB and $c$ meet Snodgrass and Corwin’s ANOVA criteria under payoffs and instructions, but do not meet them under base rates. $J$ does not meet these criteria in either Layher experiment but meets them in Measuring Memory. $B_r$ passes under payoffs but fails the Measuring Memory test on strength; $d'$ fails Layher et al.'s Experiment 1 because payoff also moves it ($F(2, 76) = 40.46$) and the two factors interact. Under the base-rate manipulation every index fails, $d'$ included, so that manipulation does not isolate bias from discriminability in these data and cannot discriminate among bias indexes.

In Experiment 1 of Layher et al. the strength differences in PPB are $+0.039$, $+0.020$ and $-0.027$ from the conservative to the liberal payoff. That is the sign pattern a constant $c$ predicts, because under EVSDT a fixed positive $c$ raises PPB as $d'$ grows and a fixed negative $c$ lowers it (main text, Definition and Properties), but the interaction is not significant ($p = .204$). The test has limited ability to separate PPB from $c$ when $d'$ changes too little to move them appreciably apart, and here the strength manipulation raised mean $d'$ from about 0.4 to about 0.8.

Sensitivity. Replacing the log-linear correction for $c$ with the $1/2N$ correction did not change whether it met the ANOVA criteria. Using raw rates for $B_r$ also left the classifications unchanged, although this required excluding two Measuring Memory participants for whom $B_r$ was undefined. For the Measuring Memory design, Type II sums of squares changed the ANOVA $F$ statistics in the first or second decimal without changing whether the criteria were met. For the within-subjects designs, the Greenhouse--Geisser lower bound, which tests every effect on 1 and 38 df and is the most conservative sphericity correction, also left the classifications unchanged.

Layher et al.'s faces are poorly discriminated (cell-mean $d'$ from 0.25 to 1.10), and strength in their Experiment 1 is confounded with practice. The Measuring Memory Project induces bias by instruction, which moved PPB less than payoffs did, and is between subjects. Neither dataset manipulates word imagery, so neither is a replication of Snodgrass and Corwin's design.

### Strength contrasts with uncertainty

{{< include tables/tbl_invariance_contrasts.md >}}

Within each bias condition the contrasts compare the highest and lowest study strength; the conservative-minus-liberal contrast compares those strength effects. The paired Layher analysis retains the covariance among each participant's cells. Measuring Memory uses independent-group means with Welch degrees of freedom. Intervals containing zero leave a range of departures unresolved. In particular, the Layher PPB difference of strength differences includes effects appreciably different from zero. Under conservative instructions in Measuring Memory, the condition-specific confidence intervals for both PPB and $c$ exclude zero even though the overall ANOVA tests detect no departure.

# Boundary Stability

## Where $c$ is undefined

$\Phi^{-1}(x)$ is defined only on $(0, 1)$, with $\Phi^{-1}(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to 0^+$ and $\Phi^{-1}(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to 1^-$. So $c$ is undefined whenever $H \in \{0, 1\}$ or $F \in \{0, 1\}$. PPB is defined and continuous everywhere on $[0, 1]^2$.

## Boundary-hitting probability

With $n_s$ signal trials and true rate $H^*$, the probability of an extreme observed rate is (the two events are mutually exclusive):

$$P(H = 0 \text{ or } H = 1) = (1 - H^*)^{n_s} + (H^*)^{n_s}$$ {#eq-boundary-prob}

| $H^*$ | $n_s$ | $P(H \in \{0, 1\})$ |
|-------|------|------|
| 0.50  |  10  | $\approx 0.002$ |
| 0.80  |  10  | $\approx 0.107$ |
| 0.90  |  10  | $\approx 0.349$ |
| 0.95  |  10  | $\approx 0.599$ |
| 0.80  |  20  | $\approx 0.012$ |
| 0.90  |  20  | $\approx 0.122$ |
| 0.95  |  20  | $\approx 0.358$ |

: Probability of a boundary hit rate ($H=0$ or $H=1$), by true rate $H^*$ and signal-trial count $n_s$. The same formula applies to $F^*$ and noise-trial count $n_n$. The main text’s total $n = 20$ is $n_s = n_n = 10$ here; $n = 40$ is $n_s = n_n = 20$. {#tbl-boundary}

@tbl-boundary gives one rate at a time. The probability of hitting *at least one* boundary across both rates follows from the independence of signal and noise trial counts:

$$P(\text{boundary}) = 1 - \big[1 - (H^*)^{n_s} - (1 - H^*)^{n_s}\big]\big[1 - (F^*)^{n_n} - (1 - F^*)^{n_n}\big]$$

## Probit sensitivity amplification

The derivative of the probit function gives the amplification factor --- how much a small perturbation $\Delta H$ in an observed rate translates into a change in $z(H)$, and hence in $c$:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\Phi^{-1}(x) = \frac{1}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(x))}$$ {#eq-probit-deriv}

| $x$ | $(\Phi^{-1})'(x)$ | Amplification relative to $x = 0.5$ |
|-----|---------|------|
| 0.50 | 2.51 | 1x (baseline) |
| 0.10 | 5.70 | 2.3x |
| 0.05 | 9.70 | 3.9x |
| 0.01 | 37.5 | 15.0x |
| 0.001 | 297 | 118x |

: Probit amplification from @eq-probit-deriv. A small perturbation $\Delta H$ near $H = 0.01$ is amplified 37.5-fold in $z(H)$ against 2.5-fold near $H = 0.50$, a relative factor of 15 (third column). For PPB, $\partial \text{PPB}/\partial H=1$ everywhere. {#tbl-amplification}

## Log-linear correction bias

The log-linear correction [@hautus_corrections_1995] replaces observed rates with:

$$H_{\text{LL}} = \frac{\text{hits} + 0.5}{n_s + 1}, \qquad F_{\text{LL}} = \frac{\text{FA} + 0.5}{n_n + 1}$$

This shrinks all rates toward 0.5 with expected bias:

$$E[H_{\text{LL}}] - H^* = \frac{0.5 - H^*}{n_s + 1}$$

Combining this shrinkage with the probit amplification (@eq-probit-deriv), the first-order effect of the correction's mean rate shrinkage on $c$ is:

$$\Delta c \approx -\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{0.5 - H^*}{(n_s + 1)\,\phi(\Phi^{-1}(H^*))} + \frac{0.5 - F^*}{(n_n + 1)\,\phi(\Phi^{-1}(F^*))}\right]$$ {#eq-correction-bias}

This expression propagates the expected change in each rate; it is not the full expected bias of a nonlinear transformed estimator. Because the probit is nonlinear, averaging transformed sample rates differs from transforming their expected rates. This contributes additional bias, so the approximation can err in either direction. At $H = 0.95$, $F = 0.20$, and $n_s = n_n = 10$, it gives $+0.150$, whereas exact expected bias is $+0.100$. The main results therefore use enumeration rather than this local approximation. With equal denominators, the shrinkage contribution in @eq-correction-bias points toward zero because $|0.5 - p| / \phi(\Phi^{-1}(p))$ increases with $|z(p)|$. With $n_s \neq n_n$ the shrinkages are weighted unequally and the sign can reverse: at $z(H) = 2$, $z(F) = -1.5$, $n_s = 1000$ and $n_n = 10$, the correction moves $c$ from $-0.25$ to $-0.33$ in expectation ($-0.40$ to first order). The corresponding distortion in PPB, from the same shrinkage without any amplification, is:

$$\Delta \text{PPB} = \frac{0.5 - H^*}{n_s + 1} + \frac{0.5 - F^*}{n_n + 1}$$

which is bounded and shrinks as $O(1/n)$, but depends on the operating point $(H^*, F^*)$. Applying the log-linear correction to PPB would introduce this bias; raw PPB requires no correction.

## The $1/2N$ correction

The $1/2N$ correction [see @macmillan_detection_1985] replaces only the extreme values: $H = 0 \mapsto 1/(2n_s)$, $H = 1 \mapsto 1 - 1/(2n_s)$. This introduces a discontinuity: a subject with $H = (n_s - 1)/n_s$ is uncorrected, while a subject with $H = 1$ jumps to $1 - 1/(2n_s)$. With $n_s = 20$, the probit value jumps from $z(0.95) = 1.645$ to $z(0.975) = 1.960$, a shift of 0.315 in $z$-space.

Both corrections produce finite estimates but can introduce finite-sample bias relative to population $c$; with equal trial counts for signal and noise, cancellation occurs when $F = 1 - H$. Raw PPB requires neither correction.

# Aggregation Discrepancy

## PPB aggregates exactly

For $K$ subjects with rates $(H_i, F_i)$:

$$\overline{\text{PPB}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_i (H_i + F_i) = \bar{H} + \bar{F} = \text{PPB}(\bar{H}, \bar{F})$$

This is an arithmetic identity for common weights: replacing $1/K$ with the same weights in both rate means and the PPB mean preserves it. Separately pooled trial rates can use different weights if individual signal and noise trial counts differ, and then need not equal the unweighted mean PPB.

## Aggregation of the normalized guess rate

For $J_i < 1$, $F_i=(1-J_i)B_{ri}$. With consistently normalized common-weight moments,

$$B_r(\bar H,\bar F)=\overline{B_r}-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(J,B_r)}{1-\bar J}$$ {#eq-br-aggregation}

Thus common $J$, common $B_r$, or zero covariance suffices for exact aggregation. $B_r$ computed from mean rates is a weighted average of individual $B_r$ values, with each observer’s original weight multiplied by $1-J_i$, the width of that observer’s uncertain region. Mean individual $B_r$ uses the original observer weights alone.

## $c$ does not aggregate exactly

$$\bar{c} = -\frac{1}{2}\left[\overline{\Phi^{-1}(H)} + \overline{\Phi^{-1}(F)}\right]$$

$$c(\bar{H}, \bar{F}) = -\frac{1}{2}\left[\Phi^{-1}(\bar{H}) + \Phi^{-1}(\bar{F})\right]$$

The discrepancy is the sum of the two transformed-rate discrepancies. Either can vanish, and nonzero contributions can cancel. Jensen's inequality determines each contribution's sign only when its rates remain within a region of fixed curvature; crossing the inflection point requires separate treatment.

## Direction and magnitude via Jensen's inequality

The probit has second derivative:

$$(\Phi^{-1})''(x) = \frac{\Phi^{-1}(x)}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(x))^2}$$ {#eq-probit-second}

This is positive for $x > 0.5$ (convex) and negative for $x < 0.5$ (concave), with an inflection at $x = 0.5$. By Jensen's inequality:

- If all rates lie above 0.5 and are not constant: $\overline{\Phi^{-1}(H)} > \Phi^{-1}(\bar{H})$
- If all rates lie below 0.5 and are not constant: $\overline{\Phi^{-1}(H)} < \Phi^{-1}(\bar{H})$

## Second-order approximation

Taylor-expanding $\Phi^{-1}(H_i)$ around $\mu_H = E[H_i]$:

$$E[\Phi^{-1}(H_i)] - \Phi^{-1}(\mu_H) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}(\Phi^{-1})''(\mu_H)\,\sigma^2_H$$

The aggregation discrepancy for $c$ is therefore approximately:

$$\bar{c} - c(\bar{H}, \bar{F}) \approx -\frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\mu_H)}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\mu_H))^2}\,\sigma^2_H + \frac{\Phi^{-1}(\mu_F)}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\mu_F))^2}\,\sigma^2_F\right]$$ {#eq-agg-approx}

The second derivative (@eq-probit-second) grows rapidly near the boundaries:

| $\mu$ | $(\Phi^{-1})''(\mu)$ |
|-------|---------|
| 0.50 | 0 |
| 0.70 | 4.34 |
| 0.80 | 10.7 |
| 0.90 | 41.6 |
| 0.95 | 155 |

: Probit second derivative used in @eq-agg-approx. Each rate’s second-order contribution to the aggregation discrepancy is proportional to its curvature times its variance. {#tbl-second-deriv}

## Worked example

Consider $K = 100$ subjects with $\mu_H = 0.90$, $\sigma_H = 0.08$ and $\mu_F = 0.15$, $\sigma_F = 0.06$. Using @eq-agg-approx:

- $H$-term: $41.6 \times 0.08^2 = 0.266$
- $F$-term: $-19.1 \times 0.06^2 = -0.069$ (negative because $\mu_F < 0.5$)

$$\bar{c} - c(\bar{H}, \bar{F}) \approx -\tfrac{1}{4}(0.266 - 0.069) = -0.049$$

$c(\mu_H, \mu_F) = -0.5[\Phi^{-1}(0.90) + \Phi^{-1}(0.15)] \approx -0.123$. The second-order approximation ($-0.049$) underestimates the simulated discrepancy ($-0.059$) because the probit's higher-order terms are non-negligible when rates are this extreme; both are a substantial fraction of the magnitude of $c$ at the population-mean rates, $c(\mu_H, \mu_F)$.

## When do the $H$ and $F$ terms cancel?

In typical applied settings, $H > 0.5$ and $F < 0.5$, so the two terms in @eq-agg-approx have opposite signs and partially cancel. When rates are symmetric about 0.5 with equal variances (e.g., $\mu_H = 0.70$, $\mu_F = 0.30$, $\sigma_H = \sigma_F = 0.08$), cancellation is nearly exact and the discrepancy is negligible. In the worked example above ($\mu_H = 0.90$, $\mu_F = 0.15$), the $F$-term offsets only 26\% of the $H$-term. Cancellation of the second-order approximation requires $(\Phi^{-1})''(\mu_H)\,\sigma^2_H = -(\Phi^{-1})''(\mu_F)\,\sigma^2_F$, which depends on the specific parameter configuration. This condition need not cancel higher-order terms. Mirrored population distributions of $H$ and $1-F$ do cancel the full expected probit contributions, but independent finite samples need not reproduce that equality.

# Covariate Effects in Probability Units

## Setup

Following @decarlo_signal_1998, who shows that signal detection models are a subclass of generalized linear models, fit separate logistic regressions for responses conditional on ground truth $b \in \{0, 1\}$:

$$\text{logit}\, P(\hat{y} = 1 \mid Y = b, x) = \eta_b(x)$$

Extract predicted rates: $\text{TPR}(x) = \sigma(\eta_1(x))$, $\text{FPR}(x) = \sigma(\eta_0(x))$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. Then:

$$\text{PPB}(x) = \sigma(\eta_1(x)) + \sigma(\eta_0(x))$$
$$c(x) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\big[\Phi^{-1}(\sigma(\eta_1(x))) + \Phi^{-1}(\sigma(\eta_0(x)))\big]$$

## Marginal effects on PPB

For a covariate $x_j$ with logistic coefficients $\beta_1^j$ (TPR model) and $\beta_0^j$ (FPR model):

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial x_j} = \sigma'(\eta_1)\,\beta_1^j + \sigma'(\eta_0)\,\beta_0^j$$ {#eq-ppb-marginal}

where $\sigma'(\eta) = \sigma(\eta)(1 - \sigma(\eta)) \in [0, 0.25]$. This is a weighted sum of the two coefficients in probability units. The weights are bounded and vary smoothly across the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) unit square.

## Marginal effects on $c$

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial x_j} = -\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\sigma'(\eta_1)\,\beta_1^j}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\sigma(\eta_1)))} + \frac{\sigma'(\eta_0)\,\beta_0^j}{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\sigma(\eta_0)))}\right]$$ {#eq-c-marginal}

The weights in @eq-c-marginal, unlike those in @eq-ppb-marginal, involve both the logistic derivative and the probit amplification factor $1/\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\cdot))$. The complete weight is $p(1-p)/\phi(\Phi^{-1}(p))$, not the reciprocal density alone. It tends to zero at either boundary: the normal-tail approximation gives a weight of order $1/|\Phi^{-1}(p)|$. Direct probability perturbations can be amplified by the probit while logit-predictor effects are simultaneously attenuated by $p(1-p)$. The finite-point example below illustrates these different units.

## Worked example

Two groups with the same logistic bias coefficient $\beta_1 = \beta_0 = 0.2$:

**Group A** (high accuracy: TPR = 0.95, FPR = 0.05):

- $\sigma'(\eta) = 0.95 \times 0.05 = 0.0475$ for both terms
- $\partial \text{PPB}/\partial x = 2 \times 0.0475 \times 0.2 = 0.019$
- $\partial c / \partial x = -0.5 \times 2 \times (0.0475/0.103) \times 0.2 = -0.092$

**Group B** (moderate accuracy: TPR = 0.75, FPR = 0.25):

- $\sigma'(\eta) = 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.1875$ for both terms
- $\partial \text{PPB}/\partial x = 2 \times 0.1875 \times 0.2 = 0.075$
- $\partial c / \partial x = -0.5 \times 2 \times (0.1875/0.318) \times 0.2 = -0.118$

The PPB effect is $0.075/0.019 \approx 4$x larger for Group B. The $c$ effect is $0.118/0.092 \approx 1.3$x larger. These ratios describe how the same logit-scale coefficient produces different effects in probability and probit units.

## Discriminability versus bias shifts

Equal logit shifts ($\beta_1^j = \beta_0^j = \delta$) give:

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial x_j} = [\sigma'(\eta_1) + \sigma'(\eta_0)]\,\delta$$

Equal-and-opposite logit shifts ($\beta_1^j = -\beta_0^j = \delta$) give:

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial x_j} = [\sigma'(\eta_1) - \sigma'(\eta_0)]\,\delta \approx 0$$

when $\sigma'(\eta_1) \approx \sigma'(\eta_0)$. $J$ and PPB are exactly orthogonal in probability space. The logistic link maps equal-and-opposite logit shifts to unequal probability shifts when $\sigma'(\eta_1) \neq \sigma'(\eta_0)$. At a symmetric operating point (TPR $= 0.95$, FPR $= 0.05$), both derivatives equal 0.0475 and the shifts leave PPB unchanged. At an asymmetric point (TPR $= 0.90$, FPR $= 0.30$), the derivatives are 0.09 and 0.21, so the shifts also change PPB.

# Sampling Theory for PPB

## Unbiasedness and variance

With $\hat{H} = X_s / n_s$ and $\hat{F} = X_n / n_n$ for independent $X_s \sim \text{Bin}(n_s, H)$ and $X_n \sim \text{Bin}(n_n, F)$,

$$E[\widehat{\text{PPB}}] = E[\hat{H}] + E[\hat{F}] = H + F = \text{PPB}$$ {#eq-ppb-unbiased}

exactly, at every $n_s$, $n_n$ and every operating point, boundaries included. Simulated "bias" in PPB is Monte Carlo error: at $H = 0.80$, $F = 0.05$, $n_s = n_n = 10$ and 5,000 simulated subjects, the Monte Carlo standard error of the mean is $\sqrt{[H(1-H)/n_s + F(1-F)/n_n] / 5000} = 0.0020$. Panel A of the main text reports exact expectations, so no such error enters it.

By independence of the signal and noise trial counts,

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\text{PPB}}) = \frac{H(1 - H)}{n_s} + \frac{F(1 - F)}{n_n}$$ {#eq-ppb-var}

A plug-in variance estimate substitutes $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{F}$ for $H$ and $F$. With fixed trial-type counts and independent trials, the pooled count of "yes" responses follows a Poisson-binomial distribution: it is a sum of independent binary responses that can have different success probabilities on signal and noise trials. It is binomial when $H=F$. With equal denominators, $\widehat{\text{PPB}}$ is a scaled pooled yes count; with unequal denominators it is a weighted sum of two binomial counts.

If trial types are instead drawn independently with signal probability $1/2$, and responses are independent with conditional probabilities $H$ and $F$, the pooled yes count is binomial with success probability $(H+F)/2$ even when $H\ne F$. The pooled yes fraction and $(\hat H+\hat F)/2$ estimate the same response probability but are generally different when the realized trial-type counts are unequal. Under random allocation, @eq-ppb-var gives the variance of $\hat H+\hat F$ conditional on the realized $n_s$ and $n_n$, provided both counts are positive. Variance across allocations with both trial types observed requires averaging over the random counts.

With fixed counts, orthogonality of the population contrasts does not imply sampling independence: $\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\text{PPB}},\hat J)=H(1-H)/n_s-F(1-F)/n_n$.

## Individual binomial intervals

A plug-in normal-approximation interval is $\widehat{\text{PPB}} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\text{PPB}})}$, without truncation to $[0, 2]$. At a boundary, a plug-in variance term is zero; this reflects the estimate, not certainty about the population probability. The interval can under-cover near boundaries and collapses when every estimated rate is extreme.

Let $C(x,n;\gamma)=[L(x,n;\gamma),U(x,n;\gamma)]$ be a two-sided Clopper--Pearson interval with confidence level $1-\gamma$ [@clopper_use_1934]. Writing $Q_B(q;a,b)$ for a beta quantile,

$$\begin{aligned}L(x,n;\gamma)&=\begin{cases}0,&x=0,\\Q_B(\gamma/2;x,n-x+1),&x>0,\end{cases}\\[1em]U(x,n;\gamma)&=\begin{cases}1,&x=n,\\Q_B(1-\gamma/2;x+1,n-x),&x<n.\end{cases}\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-cp}

Use $\gamma=\alpha/2$ for each of the signal and noise intervals. If $[L_s,U_s]$ and $[L_n,U_n]$ are those component intervals, then

$$C_{\text{PPB}}=[L_s+L_n,\ U_s+U_n]$$ {#eq-ppb-interval}

covers $H+F$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$: both component intervals cover simultaneously except on an event of probability at most $\alpha/2+\alpha/2$. This union-bound guarantee needs valid binomial marginals, but not independence between the two counts. Independence is used for the variance and exact coverage enumeration here. The interval lies in $[0,2]$, does not collapse at extreme observations, and leaves the raw point estimate unchanged. Dividing its endpoints by two gives an interval for the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation. The construction supplies a simple conservative baseline.

For two independent samples, each modeled by signal and noise binomial counts, form four component intervals, each with $\gamma=\alpha/4$. A simultaneous interval for $\text{PPB}_1-\text{PPB}_2$ is

$$[L_{s1}+L_{n1}-U_{s2}-U_{n2},\ U_{s1}+U_{n1}-L_{s2}-L_{n2}]$$ {#eq-ppb-difference-interval}

with the same union-bound guarantee under the four marginal binomial models. Rejecting equality when this interval excludes zero has a Type I error probability of at most $\alpha$. These constructions do not turn pooled trials from heterogeneous participants into a binomial sample, and do not justify an unpaired analysis of repeated conditions.

The guaranteed interval is wide at the trial counts where it is most needed. A narrower alternative is the add-one-success-and-one-failure interval that Agresti and Caffo [-@agresti_simple_2000] propose for a difference of proportions. Because $H + F = H - (1 - F) + 1$ and $1 - F$ is the proportion of noise trials without a false alarm, applying their interval to $H - (1 - F)$ and adding one gives exactly the interval below. With $\tilde H=(x_s+1)/(n_s+2)$ and $\tilde F=(x_n+1)/(n_n+2)$, the adjusted interval is

$$\begin{aligned}
&\left[\max\{0,\ \tilde H+\tilde F-z_{1-\alpha/2}\tilde s\},\ \min\{2,\ \tilde H+\tilde F+z_{1-\alpha/2}\tilde s\}\right],\\[0.5em]
&\tilde s^{2}=\frac{\tilde H(1-\tilde H)}{n_s+2}+\frac{\tilde F(1-\tilde F)}{n_n+2}
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-ppb-adjusted-interval}

Truncation to $[0,2]$ cannot lower coverage, because $H+F$ lies in that range. The interval is defined and has positive width at every observed count, but it is centered on the adjusted estimate, not on the raw $\widehat{\text{PPB}}$, and it has no coverage guarantee. At the trial counts of the grid below it contained the raw estimate for every outcome.

### Coverage and width

The interval check enumerates all pairs of binomial outcomes. Its grid crosses $n_s,n_n \in \{4,10,20\}$ with $H,F \in \{.01,.05,.10,.20,.50,.80,.90,.95,.99\}$, giving 729 configurations. Minimum coverage for the guaranteed interval was 99.36\%. For the adjusted interval, coverage averaged 97.2\% with a minimum of 91.5\% (at $H=.95$, $F=.50$, $n_s=20$, $n_n=4$) and was below 94\% in 8.4\% of configurations; its mean expected width was 0.645, against 1.024 for the guaranteed interval and 0.456 for the normal-approximation interval. The normal-approximation interval averaged 75.4\% coverage with a minimum of 7.7\%, at $H=F=.01$ and four trials per class. Coverage printed as 100.00\% is rounded, not necessarily exactly one. @tbl-interval-coverage reports exact coverage and expected width for the featured operating points, a four-trial case, and an unequal-denominator case. Width is in PPB units. The normal-approximation comparator is untruncated.

## Population and paired condition inference

When participants are sampled, $\overline{\text{PPB}}$ estimates the population mean of their conditional response sums. Its participant-level standard error is $s_{\text{PPB}}/\sqrt K$, rather than the binomial standard error obtained by treating all trials as independent and identically distributed. A t-based confidence interval uses the participant standard deviation and $K-1$ degrees of freedom. It assumes independent participants and enough participants for the approximation; repeated stimuli or other dependence may require a joint model or resampling that preserves the sampling design.

For a paired condition comparison, compute $D_i=\widehat{\text{PPB}}_{i,A}-\widehat{\text{PPB}}_{i,B}$ within each participant and use $\bar D\pm t_{K-1,1-\alpha/2}s_D/\sqrt K$. Dividing the contrast and endpoints by two gives the difference in the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation. The within-participant differences account for correlation between condition measurements; the four-component interval above applies to independent samples. The empirical worked example uses this participant-level approximation and retains every participant.

Exact aggregation identifies a population mean with the value at the same weighted mean rates. With unequal trial allocations, separate trial pools can use different participant weights and need not identify this mean. If each participant has only one trial type, population inference requires an allocation and sampling argument, such as randomized trial-type assignment to comparable participants; individual PPBs cannot be calculated from those observations. Under EVSDT, mean individual $c$ estimates average centered criterion location.

For predicted rates from covariate models, uncertainty in their sum must retain covariance between fitted rate estimates when they share participants or stimuli. Joint-model covariance or resampling at the appropriate sampling units can provide it.

# Lineup response definitions and alternative coding

The primary analysis treats choosing any lineup member as a positive response. Target-present foil choices count as positive responses under this definition, although they are incorrect identifications. Thus $J$ describes the separation in choosing rates between target-present and target-absent lineups, not identification accuracy. @tbl-lineup-responses gives every observed response category and its numerator assignment.

Under alternative perpetrator-only coding, $H$ is the proportion of all target-present trials on which the perpetrator was correctly identified, while $F$ remains the choosing proportion in target-absent trials. Target-present foil choices count as negative responses and remain in the denominator. The resulting perpetrator-only rate sum combines different response definitions across trial types and cannot be interpreted as twice the choosing probability.

The alternative perpetrator-only coding gave a pooled sum of 1.0045 instead of 1.1125, reflecting the exclusion of target-present foil choices from the $H$ numerator. Its own-minus-other sum difference was 0.0545 with a 95% paired interval of [$-0.0254$, $0.1345$]. The original study's suspect-identification ROC convention estimates innocent-suspect identifications by dividing target-absent foil identifications by lineup size [@colloff_active_2022]. Neither coding applies that adjustment.

# Group Comparisons

## Groups with similar PPB and different accuracy

The simulation generated two groups of 100 subjects, with 5,000 replications. Individual rates were drawn from beta distributions with the group means below and standard deviations of 0.04 (Group A) and 0.10 (Group B), so the simulation includes between-subject variation but no binomial trial noise and no boundary correction. Rates were clamped to $[10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]$, as in the aggregation simulation. Group A has $H = 0.95$, $F = 0.08$, PPB $= 1.03$, and $J = 0.87$; Group B has $H = 0.65$, $F = 0.40$, PPB $= 1.05$, and $J = 0.25$. The population values of $c$, computed at the group mean rates, are $-0.12$ and $-0.07$, so PPB and $c$ rank the groups in opposite directions. In the simulation, each group's PPB and $c$ were the means of the individual values, and I recorded whether the two group differences had the same sign, which means that PPB and $c$ rank the groups in opposite directions.

Observed rankings differed in 91.5\% of replications (@fig-conceptual, Panel A). The percentage depends on the group means, the between-subject spread, and the group size, and it approaches 100\% as group size increases at these population values.

## Groups matched on PPB with different latent distributions

The second simulation set PPB to 1.20 in two groups and varied the shape of their latent evidence distributions. The reference group followed an equal-variance Gaussian distribution; the comparison group followed an unequal-variance Gaussian distribution with $\sigma \in \{1.5, 2.0\}$, a logistic distribution, or a heavy-tailed $t$ distribution with 3 or 5 degrees of freedom. Every distribution had a location shift of 1.5 between the signal and noise conditions. In the unequal-variance Gaussian families, $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the signal distribution and the noise distribution has standard deviation 1. The logistic distribution has scale 1, and the $t$ distributions are unscaled: $t(3)$ has variance 3 and $t(5)$ has variance $5/3$. I found each criterion by bisection on $(-10, 10)$. These are illustrative departures from equal-variance Gaussian evidence in variance and tail behavior. Holding the location shift fixed lets discriminability vary across families. For each index (PPB, $c$, $B''$, and $B_r$), I tested the group difference with a two-sided Welch $t$ test (Satterthwaite degrees of freedom) at $\alpha = 0.05$ (200 subjects per group, 2,000 replications).

Each subject contributed 40 trials, 20 of each type. Subjects' hits and false alarms were binomial at the resulting population rates. PPB used the observed rates; $c$, $B''$ and $B_r$ used log-linearly corrected rates, so every index is defined for every subject. Algorithm `#ref(<alg-groups>, supplement: none)`{=typst} gives the procedure.

```{=typst}
#figure(
  kind: "algorithm",
  supplement: [Algorithm],
  placement: none,
  caption: [Group comparison for one pair of latent distribution families. Hit and false alarm counts are binomial with 20 trials of each type.],
  block(width: 100%, stroke: (top: 0.8pt, bottom: 0.8pt), inset: (y: 8pt, x: 4pt), align(left)[
    #set text(size: 10pt)
    #set par(leading: 0.6em, justify: false)
    *Input:* signal and noise distributions $(S_A, N_A)$ for the reference group (equal-variance Gaussian) and $(S_B, N_B)$ for the comparison family, each with location shift 1.5; target $"PPB" = 1.20$; $K = 200$ subjects per group; $R = 2000$ replications; $alpha = 0.05$ \
    #line(length: 100%, stroke: 0.4pt)
    *for* $g in {A, B}$ *do* \
    #h(1.5em) find the criterion $k_g$ such that $[1 - S_g (k_g)] + [1 - N_g (k_g)] = 1.20$ \
    #h(1.5em) $H_g <- 1 - S_g (k_g)$, #h(0.5em) $F_g <- 1 - N_g (k_g)$ \
    *end for* \
    *for* $r = 1, dots, R$ *do* \
    #h(1.5em) *for* $g in {A, B}$ *do* \
    #h(3em) *for* $i = 1, dots, K$ *do* \
    #h(4.5em) draw hits $tilde "Bin"(20, H_g)$ and false alarms $tilde "Bin"(20, F_g)$ \
    #h(4.5em) compute PPB from the observed rates \
    #h(4.5em) compute $c$, $B''$ and $B_r$ from the log-linearly corrected rates \
    #h(3em) *end for* \
    #h(1.5em) *end for* \
    #h(1.5em) for each index, run a two-sided Welch $t$ test of group $A$ against group $B$; record whether $p < alpha$ \
    *end for* \
    #line(length: 100%, stroke: 0.4pt)
    *Output:* for each index, the proportion of replications with $p < alpha$
  ])
) <alg-groups>
```

At the common PPB, $J$ ranged from 0.306 for the unequal-variance Gaussian distribution with $\sigma = 2.0$ to 0.522 for the equal-variance Gaussian distribution, a spread of 0.22; the corresponding population values of $c$ ranged from $-0.28$ to $-0.33$. Tests based on PPB maintained the nominal 5\% rejection rate because the groups had equal population PPB. Depending on the comparison distribution, $c$ detected a difference in 10\% to 75\% of replications, $B_r$ in 19\% to 100\%, and $B''$ in 33\% to 100\% (@fig-conceptual, Panel B). Across distribution families, these rejection rates followed the magnitude of the difference in $J$. Matching PPB did not match both response rates: the groups differed in $J$ and in the other bias indexes, and the higher rejection rates for the other indexes reflect differences in their population values.

# One Decision of Each Type

*Data and inclusion.* Experiments 1 to 3 of Colloff and Wixted [-@colloff_why_2020] are distributed in the pyWitness collection (`2020_Colloff_Wixted`). I kept participants coded `include == "yes"`. Participant identifiers are not unique: `subjectNo` repeats within Experiment 1, so a participant is identified by that identifier together with the random `verification` code. After this step every retained participant has exactly two decisions, one target-present and one target-absent, in a single identification condition. Conditions were showup (the witness judged a single face), simultaneous showup (the witness saw the face among five similar faces and judged only the highlighted one), and, in Experiment 3 only, a standard simultaneous lineup.

*Response.* A "Present" response is positive. In the two showup conditions this is "yes" to whether the highlighted suspect is the perpetrator. In the standard lineup it is any face choice, fillers included, so $J$ there is not suspect-identification accuracy and I omit that condition from the contrast. With one decision of each type, $H_i$ and $F_i$ are each 0 or 1, so every participant is a boundary case. @tbl-cw-conditions gives each condition's mean rates, and @tbl-cw-contrast gives the showup-minus-simultaneous-showup contrast.

{{< include tables/tbl_cw_conditions.md >}}

: Colloff and Wixted (2020), Experiments 1 to 3. Mean $H$ and $F$ are the proportions of target-present and target-absent participants responding "Present." {#tbl-cw-conditions}

{{< include tables/tbl_cw_contrast.md >}}

: Colloff and Wixted (2020): showup minus simultaneous showup differences in participant-level means of $H_i+F_i$, $J_i=H_i-F_i$, and log-linear $c_i$, with Welch 95\% intervals and two-sided Welch $p$ values. Each participant’s two decisions are kept together. Experiment 3 excludes the standard lineup. {#tbl-cw-contrast}

*Correction behavior.* With $n_s = n_n = 1$ the log-linear correction maps each rate to $(x + 1/2)/2 \in \{1/4, 3/4\}$, so $z(\tilde H_i) = (2h_i - 1)\,z_{.75}$ with $z_{.75} = \Phi^{-1}(.75)$, and likewise for $F$. Therefore

$$c_i = -\tfrac{1}{2}\left[z(\tilde H_i) + z(\tilde F_i)\right] = z_{.75}\left(1 - \text{PPB}_i\right)$$ {#eq-cw-affine}

so log-linear $c$ is an affine decreasing function of PPB, and a test of one is a test of the other, as the identical $p$ values in @tbl-cw-contrast show. The $1/2N$ correction moves every boundary rate to $1/2$ and gives $c_i = 0$ for every participant, so it cannot detect any difference. Excluding participants with a boundary rate leaves no data. Only the log-linear correction yields a usable $c$ here, and its result is PPB rescaled by $z_{.75} = 0.674$.

The present analysis uses binary responses; Colloff and Wixted’s discriminability analysis used confidence-based ROC curves. Both showup conditions asked the same suspect-identification question and differed in the faces shown and accompanying instructions. Experiment 3 also omitted the pre-identification confidence question and initial viewing delay, revised the task instructions, and randomly selected innocent suspects and fillers for each participant. The contrasts compare procedures without isolating the effects of individual changes.

# Analysis Specifications

Random number generators were seeded, and the replication archive reproduces every reported value. Scenarios within a simulation share one random stream, so reproducing a single reported scenario requires running the full sequence in the archive. In every simulation that generates trials, a subject with true rates $H$ and $F$ and $n$ total trials contributes $n_s = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ signal trials and $n_n = n - n_s$ noise trials, with hits distributed $\text{Bin}(n_s, H)$ and false alarms $\text{Bin}(n_n, F)$ independently. The log-linear correction replaces the observed rates with $(\text{hits} + 1/2)/(n_s + 1)$ and $(\text{FA} + 1/2)/(n_n + 1)$. The $1/2N$ correction replaces a rate of 0 with $1/(2m)$ and a rate of 1 with $1 - 1/(2m)$, where $m$ is the number of trials of that type, and leaves other rates unchanged.

## Boundary stability

For each configuration $(H, F, n)$ in $\{(0.80, 0.05, 20), (0.95, 0.20, 20), (0.95, 0.05, 20), (0.95, 0.10, 40)\}$, I enumerated every outcome $(h, f)$ with $0 \le h \le n_s$ and $0 \le f \le n_n$, weighted it by its binomial probability, and computed the expected value of each estimator. Bias is the expected value minus the population value, where $\text{PPB} = H + F$ and $c = -\tfrac{1}{2}[\Phi^{-1}(H) + \Phi^{-1}(F)]$. The proportion of subjects with a boundary estimate is $1 - P(0 < h < n_s)\,P(0 < f < n_n)$.

## Aggregation

Each replication drew 100 subjects with individual rates $H_i \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_H, \beta_H)$ and $F_i \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_F, \beta_F)$, drawn independently. The parameters follow from the population mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ of each rate by $\alpha = \mu\,[\mu(1-\mu)/\sigma^2 - 1]$ and $\beta = (1-\mu)\,[\mu(1-\mu)/\sigma^2 - 1]$. The three settings were

| Setting | $\mu_H$ | $\sigma_H$ | $\mu_F$ | $\sigma_F$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typical applied | 0.90 | 0.08 | 0.15 | 0.06 |
| Symmetric | 0.70 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.08 |
| Extreme | 0.95 | 0.04 | 0.05 | 0.03 |

: Means and standard deviations of the beta distributions used in the aggregation simulation. The main text reports the typical applied setting. {#tbl-agg-settings}

The individual rates are the observers' true rates, so no trials were simulated and no boundary estimates occur. Rates were clamped to $[10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]$ so that the probit is defined; this affects only the extreme tails of the beta distributions. For each index (PPB, $c$, $B''$, $B''_D$ and $B_r$), the discrepancy in a replication is the mean of the 100 individual values minus the value at the mean rates $\bar H$ and $\bar F$. The mean rates are means of the clamped values. $B''$ is set to 0 when $H = F$, and $B''_D$ to 0 when its denominator is 0. I report the average discrepancy over 2,000 replications.

## Regression

Each of two groups contained 2,000 subjects with 40 trials each ($n_s = n_n = 20$). A covariate $x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ was drawn independently for each subject. The true rates were $H_i = \sigma(\eta_1 + \beta x_i)$ and $F_i = \sigma(\eta_0 + \beta x_i)$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic function and $\beta = 0.3$ in both groups. The groups differed only in their baselines:

| Group | $\eta_1$ | $\eta_0$ | $H$ at $x = 0$ | $F$ at $x = 0$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High accuracy | 2.5 | $-2.5$ | 0.924 | 0.076 |
| Moderate accuracy | 1.0 | $-1.0$ | 0.731 | 0.269 |

: Baselines of the regression simulation. {#tbl-reg-settings}

```{=typst}
    #set text(size: 10pt)

    *Input:* baselines $eta_1, eta_0$; slope $beta = 0.3$; $N = 2000$ subjects \

    #h(1.5em) $c_i <- -1/2 [Phi^(-1)(tilde(H)_i) + Phi^(-1)(tilde(F)_i)]$ \

    *end for* \
    #line(length: 100%, stroke: 0.4pt)

```

Algorithm `#ref(<alg-regression>, supplement: none)`{=typst} gives the procedure. Adding the same quantity to both logits shifts bias on the logit scale and leaves discriminability on that scale unchanged. PPB used observed rates and $c$ used log-linearly corrected rates; all subjects were retained. The simulation is a single data set per group. The reported slope is the ordinary least squares slope of the index on $x$ within each group. A subject needed a correction if either observed rate was 0 or 1; this applied to 794 of the 2,000 high-accuracy subjects. The marginal-effect expressions above give PPB derivatives of 0.042 and 0.118 at $x=0$ in the two groups, against simulated regression slopes of 0.040 and 0.119.

I repeated the simulation with 200 other random seeds (1–200). The PPB slopes averaged 0.043 and 0.117 (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.003), and the slopes of $c$ averaged $-0.124$ and $-0.176$ (standard deviations 0.005 and 0.005). The ratio of the moderate-accuracy slope to the high-accuracy slope averaged 2.7 for PPB (standard deviation 0.14) and 1.4 for $c$ (0.07), against 3.0 and 1.6 in the reported data set. The slopes of $c$ use log-linearly corrected rates. The marginal-effect expression for uncorrected $c$ gives derivatives of $-0.147$ and $-0.179$ at $x=0$ in the two groups, a ratio of 1.2.

## Corrections, exclusion and aggregation

Take $(H, F, n) = (0.95, 0.20, 20)$ with every subject sharing the same true rates. The expected mean of log-linear-corrected $c$ over any number of subjects equals the expected value for one subject, so the enumeration above gives its bias, $+0.100$, at every group size. Excluding subjects with a boundary estimate conditions on the interior outcomes $0 < h < n_s$ and $0 < f < n_n$, and the bias of uncorrected $c$ is then $E[c \mid \text{interior}] - c$, which is 0.22 in magnitude.

## Group comparisons

For the group simulations in §7, the beta parameters follow from the stated means and standard deviations using the aggregation formula above.
